description: Hi! I’m Woan Jeng, an undergraduate student interested in coding, music, and space. I’m tackling The Earth Information Jukebox as a solo team to turn NASA’s Earth visuals into interactive audio. I am working solo and not looking for teammates right now.
summary:
EarthSonic is a web app and installable PWA that lets people hear NASA Earth science data. It pairs an interactive 3D globe and Earth visualizations with sound generated in real time in the browser using the Web Audio API, so users can explore climate and environmental change through hearing as well as sight.

For The Earth Information Jukebox challenge, EarthSonic turns documented Earth variables into sound: temperature anomaly drives pitch, and the water and atmosphere experiences drive rhythm and filter changes. A signature "Hear the Change" tool compares two moments in the same dataset and lets users hear the difference. Every dataset is labelled with its source and status (live, cached snapshot, saved on device, or demonstration data).

It matters because Earth data is mostly shared visually, which excludes blind and low-vision people and hides slow changes over time. EarthSonic also includes keyboard control, screen-reader sound descriptions, guided listening, high contrast and reduced motion. It is an independent educational project, not an official NASA product.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

EarthSonic lets users explore NASA Earth observations visually and by ear at the same time. Users pick one of three experiences, press Play, and hear a sound that follows the data as a timeline moves through the observations:

- The Warming Planet: NASA GISS global land-ocean temperature anomaly drives musical pitch.

- The Water Rhythm: water-related Earth observations drive rhythmic pulses.

- The Living Atmosphere: atmospheric observations drive filter and modulation.

Users can rotate and zoom a 3D globe, choose a location and see its place name, scrub a chart, and watch a live sound visualizer driven by the real audio output. The "Hear the Change" tool lets users pick two observations from the same dataset, see both values and their difference, and hear the sound glide from one to the other. For example, the global temperature anomaly rises from about -0.19 °C in 1956 to +1.28 °C in 2024, a difference of 1.47 °C, and users hear this as a rising pitch.

HOW IT WORKS

A Fastify backend (hosted on Render) fetches and validates NASA data (GISS GISTEMP, NASA POWER, and GIBS imagery), caches it, and serves a clean API. If a NASA source is unreachable, the server falls back to a committed snapshot of real NASA data. The React frontend (hosted on Vercel) normalizes each value to a documented 0-1 range and maps it to sound parameters (oscillator frequency, gain, filter, pulse rate), with smooth transitions and a safe master volume limit. No prerecorded music is used: all sound is synthesized live from the data values.

SCIENTIFIC TRANSPARENCY

Every dataset shows a status badge: LIVE SOURCE DATA, CACHED SOURCE SNAPSHOT, SAVED ON THIS DEVICE, or LOCAL DEMONSTRATION DATA. The badge opens details with the provider, source, retrieval time and processing steps. Missing values are never treated as zero, and percentage change is not shown for temperature anomalies because they have no absolute zero. The sound mappings are our own creative design choices, not NASA standards, and the app says so. The sound is a sonification, not real sound from Earth.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

- Makes Earth science easier to explore, understand and remember.

- Gives blind and low-vision users, and people who learn by listening, a new way to access Earth data.

- Helps students and teachers notice long-term change, such as warming, by ear.

- Works on any phone or laptop from a link, with no account or download, and can be installed as an app.

ACCESSIBILITY

We built an Accessibility Center with larger text, high contrast, a colour-blind-safe palette, a readable font, text spacing, larger controls and reduced motion. Keyboard controls work for playback, timeline and globe, and charts have text and table alternatives. Screen-reader users get text descriptions of the sound, and a Guided Listening mode so that sound and speech take turns instead of overlapping. We tested with Lighthouse, axe, automated tests and keyboard navigation. Screen-reader testing was limited, and the known gaps are listed in our repository.

TOOLS AND TECHNOLOGY

React 19, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS, Three.js (3D globe), Web Audio API, Recharts, Zod validation, Fastify (Node.js), Vitest, ESLint with jsx-a11y, axe-core, Lighthouse, vite-plugin-pwa (Workbox). Data: NASA GISS GISTEMP v4, NASA POWER (MERRA-2), and NASA GIBS imagery. Hosting: Vercel (frontend) and Render (backend). We used AI coding assistants during development, and we reviewed and tested the results ourselves.

WHAT MAKES IT CREATIVE

EarthSonic treats data as an instrument: the globe, chart and timeline all drive the sound at once, and "Hear the Change" turns decades of change into a few seconds of listening. Guided Listening is our answer to a real problem we found while testing: a screen reader talking over the sound makes both hard to understand.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

Scientific honesty (clear data status, documented ranges, no fake data), accessibility, safe audio levels (no autoplay, master volume limit), privacy (no accounts, no tracking), offline resilience (PWA and fallbacks), and performance on phones.

LINKS

Live app: https://earthsonic-six.vercel.app

Code: https://github.com/jenglee-dev/earthsonic

EarthSonic is an independent educational project created for NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. It is not an official NASA product. NASA data and visualizations remain the property of their respective owners.
